Colonies of the grey crust tunicate Diplosoma listerianum exhibit a rapid early development when maintained at a stable water temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the interval between the fertilisation of an ovum and the emergence of a free-swimming larva is quite brief, with hatching occurring just 4 days [ab = 4 days] after the zygote stage at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. This short developmental period is characteristic of many colonial ascidians that produce small, yolk-poor eggs measuring approximately 0.02 cm in diameter. The resulting newborn larvae are correspondingly diminutive, with each individual possessing a wet weight at birth of merely 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams]. Upon settling and undergoing metamorphosis, these larvae rapidly initiate feeding and begin the period of juvenile growth that follows the exotrophic transition. The temperature of 19.5 °C represents a typical summer condition for many temperate shallow-water habitats, and these values collectively define the species’ early life-history schedule under favourable environmental circumstances.

As growing juveniles progress toward their adult form, individual zooids within the colony continue to expand in size until they reach their ultimate dimensions. The fully developed zooids are cylindrical in shape, attaining a height of approximately 0.2 cm and a diameter of roughly 0.05 cm. Based on this cylindrical geometry, the calculated ultimate wet weight for a single, fully grown zooid is 0.00039 grams [Wwi = 0.00039 grams]. This modest adult body mass reflects the small scale of the constituent units that make up the encrusting colony as a whole. In the context of life-history theory, such a small adult size is often associated with rapid maturation and a relatively short overall lifespan. The entire colony, which is composed of many interconnected zooids, functions as a single physiological unit, with each zooid contributing to feeding, reproduction, and the overall maintenance of the tunicate’s gelatinous matrix. Growth rates under the standard laboratory regime of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C] are consistent and predictable, allowing for precise estimates of subsequent life-cycle transitions.

Sexual maturation in Diplosoma listerianum follows a defined schedule that is tightly linked to colony age and prevailing temperature. At the reference temperature of 19.5 °C, the period from the time of larval settlement until the initial onset of gonadal activity is approximately 50 days from the time of larval settlement [tp = approximately 50 days from the time of larval settlement] at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. This milestone marks the point at which individual zooids become reproductively viable, producing the first generation of gametes. The timing of this transition appears closely associated with the regression of the colony that occurs shortly after the liberation of the first brood of larvae, a phenomenon that has been noted in several colonial tunicates. The total lifespan of the colony, from the settlement of the founding larva to the eventual senescence and natural mortality of all its constituent zooids, is documented to be 90 days [am = 90 days] under these same stable thermal conditions at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. This relatively compressed life cycle, with a brief juvenile phase followed by a concentrated period of reproduction, is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy adapted to ephemeral substrates in shallow coastal environments.

Reproductive output in Diplosoma listerianum has been quantified through detailed laboratory observations of actively breeding colonies. Each mature zooid releases tadpole larvae continuously throughout its reproductive window, with an estimated maximum output of roughly 60 larvae per zooid per year [Ri = roughly 60 larvae per zooid per year]. This per-zooid fecundity is modest when considered in isolation, but the colonial nature of the organism means that total colony output is multiplied by the number of simultaneously reproductive zooids. The production of these larvae occurs continuously from the onset of puberty until the senescence of the colony, rather than in distinct seasonal pulses, which may buffer the population against stochastic mortality events in the planktonic phase. The measured rates were all obtained at the standard experimental temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C].

Field observations of Diplosoma listerianum from various coastal sites corroborate the laboratory-derived life-history schedule, with some interesting geographic variation. The 90-day life span (90 days) [am = 90 days] measured under controlled conditions is broadly consistent with estimates from natural populations, although actual longevity in the field may be truncated by predation or overgrowth by competing sessile organisms at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. The wet weight at birth of 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams] aligns well with calculations based on the measured egg diameter of 0.02 cm, confirming the absence of significant post-ovulatory enlargement. Interestingly, the age at puberty of 50 days from the time of larval settlement [tp = 50 days from the time of larval settlement] observed at 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C] can be extended by several weeks in cooler waters, illustrating a direct thermal dependence of maturation timing. The maximum reproductive potential of 60 larvae per zooid per year [Ri = 60 larvae per zooid per year] suggests that even a moderate-sized colony with several dozen fertile zooids can contribute substantially to local larval supply, underpinning the species’ capacity for rapid colonization of new substrates.
